content_text: this article needs a Part Two, but the message in Part One here should carry a shitload of weight for a jr/mid-level analyst. I think I can break it down for you here into 7 parts. 1. The main question being answered here is, "how do I learn a new stock?" There are a billion responses, none are the same, and the major issue is that it is VERY easy to spin your wheels and spend an awful lot of time on shit that doesn't matter. The goal is to adopt Munger's mindset of what is basically 80/20 rule. He has his mental models, his latticework, where he has say 100 frameworks that he uses. These 100 frameworks do not capture 100% of the universe. However, they capture 80%, and he is okay with that, because there is an implicit Return on Time calculation here. Like, he has optimized for the least amount of baggage, that allows him to slice through 80% of the world with 80% accuracy. He's fine missing those last 20%'s. The incremental Return on Time falls off a cliff, or he knows that he grasps the "meat" of an issue, et cetera. That's what this is all about. 2. TL;DR Version of Article Real quick, I'll give the short answer here and then a longer answer in support. The short answer, which is detailed in the article, is these three things: I. Build a model, quarterly, going back 20 years minimum. II. Read every earnings transcript going back 20 years. III. Grind the daily stock chart going back 20 years. You do all three of these at the same time, starting from present day and going backwards, quarter by quarter. I have tried a LOT of shit over the years, and I believe these three steps are the optimal 80/20. Remember, no 80/20 is perfect. This trifecta, to me, gets you the deepest familiarity with a business in the aspects that matter -- the ones that actually move the needle on P&L. 3. "What Matters?" The model is straightforward, you should always have 2008-2009 in there (aka back 20 years) to know how a biz responds in a shitstorm. The 80/20 rule applies to modeling more than anything -- I think I've spoken to this at length in the Modeling articles in my pinned tweet, some examples of what can be combined/excluded. Here, meanwhile, the earnings transcripts and the chart will show you what drives the STOCK PRICE. You'll learn about management too, but your goal here is to understand the P&L in a way that connects to how the stock trades on quarters and catalysts. Every single gap on that stock chart, you are going to know cold what drove it. Everything is 80/20 rule, every stock has 2-3 KPI's that matter more than the rest and which create volatility on prints. This trifecta approach will show you exactly which line items are behind every explosive move on the chart for the last 20 years. The article has more. Here, I will give context around this general approach and save the rest for Part Two. The last thing I'd add, is that your goal, as usual, is to be the smartest guy in the room on your sector and each individual business. This trifecta is going to dial you in quickly, because earnings transcripts (and the Q&A) are wonderful in illustrating how management thinks about the business, and in showing you how the P&L reacts to changes in the business cycle. 4. The Other Items The reason these are tricky posts is that it is incumbent on me to touch on all the other guys' checklist items, and explain why I 80/20'd them where I did, or where I stand on them...it's always a judgment call as far as what you leave out. But the point of this post, or repost, is to plant this trifecta in the mind of someone who just read 100 checklists, most of which are written by busywork purist types ("read every single SEC filing ever!") and which have no tie to P&L. There is a ruthless mentality here and a willingness to go against the crowd. Because someone will say "oh, how can you NOT recommend that an analyst read every single SEC filings?" FWIW, there is very high overlap between this guy and "long-term quality investor" guy. Like, he's going to try and moralize this process, as if reading every proxy statement negates the fact that he's in a 60% drawdown. So I will take my time and touch on every possible item. It's not that filings, street notes, expert calls, etc don't matter -- it's that I believe your first three steps, before you do anything else, should be the triumvirate I laid out above. I believe this ~10-20 hour process for ramping on a new name has the strongest tie to P&L/risk management and gets you in the driver's seat, in the shortest amount of time, to where you are "war-ready" and know exactly what drives the stock price. Because that's all we care about. Your P&L is calculated off the stock price, not last year's ROIC, not Morningstar's Wide Moat Rating, not even any of the shit in Excel. We want to know what 2-3 KPI's make this bitch sing, 80/20 those, and speedrun the rest of the model. 5. A ton of L/S equity, especially multi-mgr L/S equity, is driven by this exact principle. I call it Return on Time. I don't know if I made this up or where I got it from but its straightforward and you know exactly what I mean. I would say Return on Time it is the #1 trait that differentiates an average from a great analyst/PM -- they have a mind like a thresher. This absolutely applies for modeling as well, it applies for every aspect of the job. The sooner you can start rewiring your mind towards this endgoal, the better. The great analyst is able to take 100 pieces of new information, and then immediately wage all-out war on this info with their version of Munger's mental arsenal. In a shockingly brief amount of time, they're left holding 2 pages, and it's the exact 2 that matter. What happened to the rest? Off the rip, they knew which 20 could be shredded, which 20 could be skipped, which could be shortcutted via pattern recognition...shit like that. This part takes time. There is also work that they have done tying each piece info to not just "Does this matter," but "process vs. outcome" -- meaning, does this part of my process generate excess returns, green P&L, or am I engaging in pointless busywork? Like I said - there is a ruthlessness here, an individuality, and most importantly, an inward-facing mentality: "Has this specific step been proven to help me generate P&L?" If not, throw it in the trash. No sacred cows. 6. Bonus Tip: Observe Bad Analysts Stephen King says you learn more reading bad books than good ones. I absolutely believe you can learn how to be a great analyst by watching a shitty or average one, watch how they spend their time, how they prioritize (or don't), how they think about outcomes (P&L) vs. process (or not). You can ask a guy why he does something and he'll tell you it's because he read that Seth Klarman does it, 15 years ago. And he's still doing it because he's "smart" and even if he can't make money, he can "be right." This is busywork. You want to eliminate any and all busywork. 7. Next Steps I feel very comfortable advising any analyst who is aged 20-30 and trying to learn a new sector, to roll with the three steps I have laid out. Each company is time-consuming. But you only have to do this once, the 20-year lookback, and then it permanently lodges itself in your mind. I told a 20-year old guy to just pick 10 businesses that he wants to learn cold, and do this process for each of them. Those 10, you'll have those for life, they may even end up being your go-to stock pitches. The reason why I have high conviction in these three steps is that you are never going to regret doing any of them. I have never once regretted uploading a business to my brain (say 10-20 hours) even if I never looked at it again. Because it's all cumulative knowledge. Let's say 20 stocks is 400 hours, those are 400 of the highest possible Return on Time hours I can imagine. I have no qualms telling someone to "go do their 400" and gauge their passion based on their progress. I know what their alternative is, they're getting jerked around by some shitty "Official Research Process Checklist" and getting 0 hours, when they just need to get smacked in the face and told: there are 400 solid gold hours for you right here, right now. So... I view these 3 steps as 0% fat. There is no excess here. You have zero risk of getting bogged down in 10-K depreciation schedules or other shit that is not immediately helping you ramp on a stock, on a sector, and on trading markets in general. Each rep in each of these three steps is dynamite: I. Model reps. 100% unavoidable, every rep is money. II. Transcripts, get a feel for management, what the street is keyed in on, the narrative, and the P&L sensitivity throughout all the ups and downs. III. And of course, the highest Return on Time of them all...grinding stock charts like you're Stan Druckenmiller at 4:30 AM each morning. The chart reps are the unspoken hero. They are what set you up long-term for the analyst --> PM transition, as you develop both tape feel and subconscious pattern recognition. Model on one side, transcript on the other, connecting the three in your mind, three months at a time, as you become fluent in a new business. END: The Dark Room I am fond of saying that "all man's greatness is built when he is in a dark, quiet room, all alone." The hours that nobody will ever see or know about, driven by passion for the game, where you aren't even aware that time is passing...you're just all by your lonesome, dreaming of title belts, and "breaking down tape" as if you were Luke motherfucking Kuechly. Just shit winners do. In the meantime, if you are ever overcome with a spontaneous desire for self-improvement, "go do 400." The goal is to be the smartest person in the world on your businesses, and this is the exact process that gets you there...one business at a time, hour by hour, quarter by quarter, and brick by brick. hth
